Labour: Centre-left party founded in 1900 with roots in the trade union movement.
Conservative: Centre-right party whose modern form dates from the 1830s. Its members are often called Tories.
Liberal Democrats: Centrist, liberal party formed in 1988 by the merger of the Liberal Party and the Social Democratic Party.
SNP: Founded in 1934. Campaigns for Scottish independence.
Reform UK: Right-wing party founded in 2018 as the Brexit Party and renamed Reform UK in 2021.
Green: Green Party of England and Wales
Environmentalist party, separate from the Scottish Greens since 1990.
DUP: Northern Ireland unionist party founded in 1971.
Sinn Féin: Irish republican party. Its MPs do not take their seats in the House of Commons.
SDLP: Northern Ireland nationalist party founded in 1970.
Alliance: Northern Ireland party founded in 1970 that does not identify as unionist or nationalist.
UUP: Northern Ireland unionist party founded in 1905.
TUV: Northern Ireland unionist party founded in 2007.
Independent: Not a member of any political party.
Speaker: Speaker
The Speaker gives up party ties while in the chair.
Non-affiliated: Members of the House of Lords who belong neither to a political party nor to the Crossbench group (House of Commons Library briefing CBP-10635).
Crossbench: Peers who belong to no party and sit independently in the House of Lords.
Lords Spiritual: Church of England bishops who sit in the House of Lords because of their office.

person.blurb: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom since 2026

children.electedBy: Appointed by the monarch as the person most likely to command the confidence of the House of Commons, in practice the leader of the largest party or of a coalition. By convention the Prime Minister sits in the Commons. Voters do not elect the Prime Minister directly.
children.reportsTo: The monarch, who appoints them, and the House of Commons, which can remove the government with a vote of no confidence.
children.plain: The head of government. Leads the Cabinet, chooses (and can dismiss) the other ministers and runs the government day to day. Stays in office only while commanding the confidence of the House of Commons.
plainFacts: No fixed term; a general election is due within five years of Parliament first meeting
The monarch, on the basis of Commons support
A Commons vote of no confidence, an election defeat, or their own resignation
The most executive power in the country
terms: Confidence vote
A Commons vote on whether the government still has majority support. Losing one normally means resigning or an election.
Majority mark
326 of the 650 seats: the number a party needs to win every vote on its own.

person.name: Charles III
person.blurb: King of the United Kingdom since 2022

children.electedBy: Hereditary. The crown passes by birth, mainly to the sovereign's eldest child, under rules in the Act of Settlement 1701 and the Succession to the Crown Act 2013.
children.reportsTo: Head of state. Acts on the advice of ministers rather than answering to voters.
children.plain: The head of state. By long-standing convention the monarch takes no political decisions: the powers of the Crown are used on the advice of ministers. The monarch appoints the Prime Minister (the person who can command the confidence of the House of Commons), gives Royal Assent to bills and formally opens each session of Parliament.
plainFacts: Cannot be removed; can only abdicate, which needs an Act of Parliament
Mostly ceremonial; ministers use the Crown's powers
terms: Royal Assent
The monarch's formal approval that turns a bill passed by Parliament into law.
Royal prerogative
Powers of the Crown that ministers exercise in the monarch's name, such as making treaties.

children.sub: House of Commons · Speaker Lindsay Hoyle
children.electedBy: 650 members, each elected by the voters of one constituency under first-past-the-post. A general election must be held within five years of Parliament first meeting, and the Prime Minister can ask the monarch to call one earlier.
children.reportsTo: The voters. The government stays in power only while it keeps the confidence of this house.
children.plain: The elected chamber of Parliament and the seat of political power. Passes laws together with the House of Lords, approves taxes and spending, questions ministers and can bring down a government with a vote of no confidence. The Commons has the final say if the two houses disagree.
terms: First-past-the-post
The candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority of all votes.
Constituency
The area whose voters elect one MP.
Speaker
The MP who chairs debates and keeps order. Gives up party ties while in the chair.

memberPlain.plain: Elected by the voters of one constituency to sit in the House of Commons. MPs debate and vote on laws, question ministers and represent local people. The party or coalition that holds most seats forms the government.
facts: Losing an election, resigning, or disqualification such as a prison sentence of more than a year
terms: First-past-the-post
The candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority of all votes.

children.sub: House of Lords · Lord Speaker Lord Forsyth of Drumlean
children.electedBy: Not elected. The Lords Temporal are life peers appointed by the monarch on the Prime Minister's advice, plus up to 26 Church of England bishops who sit by right of office. Hereditary peers lost their right to sit in April 2026.
children.reportsTo: Parliament. It revises the Commons' bills but cannot override the elected house.
children.plain: The unelected second chamber of Parliament. It examines and amends bills passed by the Commons and can delay most of them for about a year, but the Commons has the final say. Members are appointed rather than elected.
plainFacts: 796 with status "Current Member" in the Parliament Members API; excludes 19 peers on leave of absence (16), disqualified (2) or suspended (1)
terms: Life peer
A member appointed for life who cannot pass the title on to their children.
Lords Spiritual
Church of England bishops with seats in the Lords because of their position.
Crossbencher
A peer who belongs to no party.

memberPlain.plain: A member of the House of Lords: a life peer or a Church of England bishop. Lords debate and amend bills, question the government and serve on committees. They are not elected and do not represent a constituency.
facts: For life (bishops until they retire as bishops)
Appointment by the monarch on advice
Retiring, or expulsion for serious misconduct or crime

children.electedBy: An independent selection commission picks one candidate for each vacancy. The Lord Chancellor can accept or reject the choice, and the Prime Minister then recommends the appointment to the monarch. Justices serve until the mandatory retirement age of 75.
children.reportsTo: The law only. Independent of the government and Parliament.
children.plain: The final court of appeal for civil cases across the UK and for criminal cases from England, Wales and Northern Ireland. It decides legal questions of general public importance and rules on disputes about the powers of the devolved governments. It cannot strike down Acts of Parliament.

terms: Devolution
The transfer of some powers to the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland governments.

root.place: Government and Parliament of the UK
root.summary: A parliamentary constitutional monarchy. The monarch is head of state but acts on ministers' advice; the Prime Minister leads the government, which must keep the confidence of the elected House of Commons. Parliament (Commons and Lords) makes laws, and the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal.
root.plain: A parliamentary constitutional monarchy. The monarch is head of state but acts on ministers' advice; the Prime Minister leads the government, which must keep the confidence of the elected House of Commons. Parliament (Commons and Lords) makes laws, and the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal.
plainFacts: House of Commons (650) and House of Lords
root.electedBy: The UK has no single written constitution. It is set out in Acts of Parliament, court decisions and conventions. Voters elect the House of Commons, and the government is formed from the party or coalition that can win the Commons' confidence.
root.reportsTo: The voters, through the House of Commons
